unit.title: Operate computer aided design (CAD) to produce basic drawing elements

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and use a CAD workstation safely, to avoid eye strain, back and wrist problems and electrical hazards.
essays.modelAnswer: Adjust the chair so that your feet are flat on the floor or on a footrest, your back is supported and your thighs are about level. The desk height should let your forearms rest about level, with relaxed shoulders and straight wrists. Put the screen straight in front of you, about an arm's length away, with the top of the screen at or a little below eye level. Set the brightness and text size so you can read easily, and place the screen so that windows and lights do not shine on it. Keep the mouse close to the keyboard so you do not stretch. Take short breaks, about 5 to 10 minutes every hour, and every 20 minutes or so look at something far away to rest your eyes. For electrical safety, check that cables and plugs are not damaged, do not overload power strips, keep drinks away from the computer, and keep cables tidy so that no one trips. Report any damaged equipment and do not use it.
markingPoints: Chair adjusted: feet flat, back supported
Forearms level, wrists straight, mouse close to the keyboard
Screen in front at arm's length, top at or a little below eye level, no glare
Regular short breaks and rest for the eyes
Electrical safety: check cables and plugs, no overloading, no drinks, tidy cables, report damage

essays.stem: Explain absolute, relative and polar coordinate entry in CAD, with an example of each for drawing a line.
essays.modelAnswer: Coordinates tell the CAD program exactly where a point is, using X for the distance across and Y for the distance up from the origin, the point 0,0. Absolute coordinates are always measured from the origin. For example, if a line starts at 20,20 and you type 120,20, the line ends 100 mm to the right, because both points are measured from 0,0. Relative coordinates are measured from the last point you picked, and are usually typed with the @ sign in front. For example, after starting at 20,20, typing @100,0 draws a line 100 mm to the right, and then typing @0,50 draws a line 50 mm straight up from that end. Polar coordinates are also measured from the last point, but you give a distance and an angle instead of X and Y. For example, a distance of 80 mm at an angle of 30° draws an 80 mm line sloping up to the right. Angles are measured anticlockwise from the 3 o'clock direction. Relative and polar entry are the quickest for most drawing work.
markingPoints: X across and Y up, measured from the origin 0,0
Absolute: measured from the origin, with a correct example
Relative: measured from the last point using @, with a correct example
Polar: a distance and an angle from the last point, with a correct example
Angles measured anticlockwise from 3 o'clock (positive X)

essays.stem: Describe how to set up a new CAD drawing for a steel part, before you start drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: Start a new drawing from the Centre's template if there is one, because it already has the right settings. Check that the units are set to millimetres, with the decimal places to suit the job, and that angles are in degrees. Set the drawing limits or work area to fit the part at full size, and turn on a grid and snap at a useful spacing such as 10 mm. Create the layers you will need, each with a clear name, colour, linetype and lineweight: for example Outline (continuous, thick), Hidden (dashed, thin), Centre (chain, thin), Dimensions and Text (thin) and Title block. Set up a text style with a clear font and a suitable height, and a dimension style with the right text height, arrow size and units. Insert the title block and fill in the job details. Save the file straight away with a clear name, such as the job number and part name, in the right folder, and keep saving as you work.
markingPoints: Starts from the template; units in mm, decimal places and angles set
Work area or limits, grid and snap set
Layers created with names, colours, linetypes and lineweights
Text style and dimension style set
Title block inserted; file saved at once with a clear name in the right folder

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would draw a rectangular plate 100 mm × 60 mm with 10 mm radius corners and four 12 mm diameter holes, each 15 mm in from both edges.
essays.modelAnswer: Set the Outline layer as current. Use the Rectangle command: pick the first corner at 0,0 and type @100,60 for the opposite corner, which gives a 100 mm × 60 mm rectangle. Use the Fillet command, set the radius to 10 mm, and pick the two sides at each corner to round all four corners. Next, find the hole centres. Change to the Centre layer and use Offset to draw lines 15 mm in from each edge, or use the coordinates of the centres: 15,15, 85,15, 85,45 and 15,45. Change back to the Outline layer and draw a circle of 12 mm diameter (6 mm radius) at the first centre, snapping to the intersection of the centre lines. Copy the circle to the other three centres using object snaps, or use a rectangular array of 2 rows and 2 columns with spacings of 70 mm and 30 mm. Trim the centre lines so they go a little past each hole. Check the sizes with the distance tool, add dimensions on the Dimensions layer and save the drawing.
markingPoints: Rectangle drawn accurately (for example 0,0 then @100,60) on the outline layer
Fillet with a 10 mm radius on all four corners
Hole centres found correctly (15,15 85,15 85,45 15,45) by offset or coordinates
12 mm diameter circles placed with object snaps; copied or arrayed at 70 mm and 30 mm spacing
Centre lines tidied, sizes checked, dimensioned and saved

essays.stem: Explain why layers are used in CAD, and describe a sensible layer set-up for a mechanical drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: Layers work like clear sheets laid on top of each other. Each type of object is drawn on its own layer, so it can be controlled as a group. A layer can be turned off or frozen to hide it, locked so that its objects can be seen but not changed, and given its own colour, linetype and lineweight, so that the objects on it look right on screen and when printed. This makes the drawing easier to work on and to check, and gives the right line types without setting each object one by one. A sensible set-up for a mechanical drawing is: Outline, with a continuous linetype and a thick lineweight, for visible edges; Hidden, dashed and thin; Centre, chain and thin; Dimensions and Text, thin, in their own colour; Hatching, thin; Construction, for temporary lines, turned off before printing; and Title block, locked so that it is not moved by mistake. Always check which layer is current before you draw.
markingPoints: Layers group objects so each group can be controlled
On or off, freeze and lock explained
Colour, linetype and lineweight set by layer so that lines print correctly
Sensible named layers: outline, hidden, centre, dimensions or text, hatching, title block
Construction layer turned off for printing, or the current layer checked before drawing

essays.stem: Explain how you would use editing commands to turn a rough outline into a finished part outline. Name at least four commands and say what each one does.
essays.modelAnswer: A rough outline is often drawn quickly, with lines that cross over or stop short, so editing commands are used to make it neat and accurate. Trim cuts off the parts of lines that go past a cutting edge, such as where two lines cross at a corner. Extend lengthens a line that stops short so that it meets a boundary line. Offset makes a parallel copy at an exact distance, for example the inside edge of a frame 5 mm in from the outside, or a centre line 15 mm in from an edge. Fillet joins two lines with a rounded corner of a set radius, and with a radius of 0 it makes a clean, sharp corner. Chamfer makes an angled corner instead. Move and Copy place objects exactly, using a base point and object snaps, and Mirror copies half of a symmetrical part to make the whole. Erase removes construction lines that are no longer needed. After editing, check the sizes with the distance tool before adding dimensions.
markingPoints: Trim — cuts lines back to a cutting edge
Extend — lengthens a line to meet a boundary
Offset — a parallel copy at an exact distance
Fillet or chamfer — rounded or angled corners (fillet radius 0 for a sharp corner)
Other correct commands (move, copy, mirror, erase), and sizes checked afterwards

essays.stem: Describe how to add dimensions and notes to a CAD drawing so that it can be used in the workshop.
essays.modelAnswer: First check that the drawing is correct and drawn at full size, because the dimensions measure the objects themselves. Set the Dimensions layer as current, and use a dimension style with a clear text height, about 3.5 mm on the printed sheet, neat arrows and millimetre units. Use object snaps so that each dimension picks up the exact end points and centres. Use linear dimensions for horizontal and vertical sizes, aligned dimensions for sloping edges, diameter dimensions for holes, radius dimensions for arcs and rounded corners, and angular dimensions for angles. Place the dimensions outside the views where possible, give each size once only, and dimension holes from a datum edge. Keep the dimensions associative, so that they update if the part is changed. Add notes on the Text layer, such as the material, the thickness, ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM, the general tolerance and any welding notes. Fill in the title block. Finally, use print preview to check that all the text can be read and that no dimensions cross each other.
markingPoints: Dimensions layer and a suitable dimension style (text about 3.5 mm, mm units)
Object snaps used so that dimensions pick exact points
Correct dimension types: linear, aligned, diameter, radius, angular
Good practice: outside the views, each size once, from a datum, associative
Notes and title block completed, and checked in print preview

essays.stem: Describe the steps to print a CAD drawing to scale on A3 paper, and how you check that the printed scale is right.
essays.modelAnswer: Save the drawing first. Open the print (plot) settings, or the layout set up for printing. Choose the printer, the paper size, A3, and the direction, landscape or portrait, to suit the drawing. Choose what to print, such as the layout, the extents of the drawing or a window around the title block. Set the scale, for example 1:1 or 1:2, instead of fit to paper, because fit to paper gives an odd scale that cannot be measured. Check that the line weights and colours are set to print correctly, usually in black with thick and thin lines. Centre the drawing on the paper. Use print preview to check that everything fits inside the border and that the text can be read. Then print. To check the scale, measure a known dimension on the printed sheet with a rule. For example, a 200 mm line printed at 1:2 should measure 100 mm. Make sure the scale in the title block matches. If the size is wrong, check the scale setting and print again.
markingPoints: Printer, A3 paper size and direction chosen
Area to print chosen and a set scale used, not fit to paper
Line weights or colours set to print correctly; drawing centred
Print preview used before printing
Scale checked by measuring a known dimension (for example 200 mm at 1:2 = 100 mm); title block scale matches

essays.stem: Explain good file management for CAD work, including naming, folders, saving, backup and drawing revisions.
essays.modelAnswer: Every drawing file needs a clear name that tells what it is, such as the job number, the part name and the drawing number, for example J104-base-plate-D01. Avoid names like Drawing1, which are easily lost or written over. Keep files in an organised set of folders, for example one folder for each job or customer, and save them in the shared folder the Centre uses, not on the desktop. Save the file as soon as you start, and then save often while working, because a power cut or a crash can lose hours of work. Use Save As to make a new version rather than writing over an approved drawing. Keep backups: a copy on another drive, a memory stick or the Centre's backup system, updated regularly. When a drawing is changed after it has been issued, change the revision letter, for example from A to B, write what was changed and the date in the revision table, and save it as a new revision so that the old one is kept for the record.
markingPoints: Clear file names with job number, part name and drawing number
Organised folders in the correct shared place
Save early and often; Save As for new versions
Regular backups kept in another place
Revisions: letter changed, change and date noted, old revision kept

essays.stem: Compare producing a mechanical drawing with CAD and by hand on a drawing board. Give advantages of each.
essays.modelAnswer: CAD has many advantages. It is very accurate, because sizes are typed in and points are picked with object snaps. Changes are quick: a line can be moved or a hole added without redrawing the whole sheet. Parts that repeat, such as bolt holes or title blocks, can be copied, arrayed or inserted as blocks. The same drawing can be printed at different scales, sent by email as a PDF, and stored safely with backups. Layers and dimension tools give neat, even line types and lettering every time. Drawing by hand also has advantages. The equipment is cheap and needs no power, so it can be used anywhere, even in the workshop or on site. It is quick for a simple sketch or a one-off idea. Learning to draw by hand also teaches the projection and dimensioning rules well, which helps when using CAD. However, hand drawing is slower to change and to copy, and its accuracy depends on the skill of the person drawing.
markingPoints: CAD: accurate sizes from typed values and snaps
CAD: quick to change, copy and reuse (blocks, arrays)
CAD: print at any scale, share and store electronically with backups
Hand: cheap, no power needed, quick for simple sketches
Hand: builds understanding of drawing rules, but slower to change

practical1.title: Draw and dimension a base plate in CAD using coordinates, layers and editing commands
practical1.brief: Each member of the group works at their own CAD workstation and draws the same base plate from a sketch the instructor gives: a 150 mm × 100 mm plate with 10 mm radius corners, four 14 mm diameter holes 20 mm in from both edges, and a 40 mm diameter centre hole, all with centre lines. Each member sets up the drawing (millimetres, and layers for outline, centre lines and dimensions), draws the outline using typed coordinates, uses fillet, offset or coordinates, object snaps and copy or array for the holes, adds dimensions, and saves the file with the group's naming rule in the group folder. Members take turns to check a neighbour's sizes with the distance tool. Take a phone photo of your own screen at each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A computer for each member with the Centre's CAD program and drawing template
The instructor's sketch of the base plate
A group folder on the Centre's network or a memory stick
A phone or camera for screen photos
photos: The layer list on screen, showing the layers each member made
The outline drawn, with the typed coordinates showing on the command line
The corners filleted, and the holes and centre lines drawn
The finished, dimensioned base plate on screen
The file saved in the group folder with the correct name (the file window on screen)
A member checking a neighbour's size with the distance tool
checklist: Set the units to millimetres and made correctly named layers with suitable linetypes
Drew the outline accurately using typed coordinates
Used object snaps and editing commands (fillet, offset, copy or array) correctly
Holes are the right size and in the right places, with centre lines on the correct layer
Added clear, correct dimensions on the dimensions layer
Saved the file with the correct name in the group folder
Sat with good posture and took a short break during the session
safety: Adjust the chair and screen before starting; keep the top of the screen at or a little below eye level
Take a short break at least once an hour and rest your eyes
Keep drinks away from the computers and keep cables tidy
Do not use damaged cables or plugs; report them to the instructor

practical2.title: Produce and print a two-view drawing of an angle bracket with a title block, to scale
practical2.brief: Each member of the group draws a steel angle bracket from the instructor's sketch: 75 mm × 75 mm × 6 mm angle, 100 mm long, with two 12 mm holes in each leg. Draw a front view and an end view (or a plan) lined up with each other, on the right layers, with hidden lines and centre lines where they are needed. Insert or draw a title block and fill it in with the title, name, date, scale, material and projection. Set up the print for A4 or A3 at a stated scale, check it in print preview, print it, and measure one dimension on the paper to check the scale. Members share the printer and check each other's prints. Take a phone photo of the screen and of the printed drawing at each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with every member's printed drawing.
materials: A computer for each member with the Centre's CAD program
The instructor's sketch of the angle bracket
A printer with A4 or A3 paper
A steel rule or scale rule for checking the print
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The two views drawn on screen, lined up with each other
The title block filled in, on screen
The print settings or print preview, showing the paper size and scale
The printed drawing on the desk
A rule measuring a dimension on the printed drawing
Every member's printed drawing laid out together
checklist: Drew both views accurately and lined them up with each other
Used the correct layers and line types for outlines, hidden lines and centre lines
Added correct dimensions and notes that can be read when printed
Filled in the title block, including the scale and the projection
Set a stated print scale (not fit to paper) and checked it in print preview
Checked the printed scale correctly by measuring a dimension
Saved the drawing with the correct name before printing
safety: Set up the workstation with good posture before starting
Take short breaks and rest your eyes
Keep fingers out of the printer; clear paper jams only as the maker's instructions say
Keep drinks away from the computers and printer, and keep cables tidy
